item.title: New Scientist: What is the electrification target at COP31 and can countries meet it?
item.description: The world will need to quadruple its pace on electrification to meet the target being pushed by the COP31 presidency this week, but increasingly affordable renewable energy could put the goal within reach

item.title: Nature: California votes to give record $8.4 billion to medical research
item.description: Nature, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03635-6 The cash infusion, earmarked for immunology studies, is the largest ever for science authorized by a US public vote — but it has drawn criticism.

item.title: New Scientist: A science fiction novel has finally won the Booker prize. It’s about time
item.description: The literary world has long been reluctant to allow science fiction works into the starry ranks of literary fiction. Will M. John Harrison’s landmark win for The End of Everything finally change that?

item.title: Nature: A practically perfect plesiosaur
item.description: Nature, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03278-7 A very well preserved ancient marine reptile and a Latin poem that describes an optical phenomenon, in this week’s pick from the Nature archive.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03589-9 Clues from Mongolia suggest that underground fungal networks might be key for reviving degraded land and preserving plant biodiversity.

item.title: Nature: The public trusts scientists with AI — more than it does anyone else
item.description: Nature, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03578-y Public confidence in scientists’ use of generative artificial intelligence remains high, but that trust comes with conditions.

item.title: Nature: Some people are resistant to dementia — here’s what their genes can teach us
item.description: Nature, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03625-8 For years, researchers have studied people with a genetic predisposition to Alzheimer’s and other dementias. They might have even more to learn from those who don’t get the disease.

item.title: New Scientist: Newly described insect may live its whole life on a spider’s web
item.description: A species of “web-loving bug” from China lives on a spider's web and seems to follow its arachnid host around. The insect may be too small for the spider to bother attacking

item.description: Nature, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03623-w Picking a site for an observatory should be about more than science. Humanities scholars have a crucial role in responsible siting.

item.title: Nature: How microbes can secure the critical minerals the world needs
item.description: Nature, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03629-4 To sustain supplies of key metals, policymakers should support the infrastructure needed to deploy mining biotechnologies on a large scale.

item.title: New Scientist: How neutrinos are beginning to reveal the secrets of our galaxy
item.description: Columnist Chanda Prescod-Weinstein says understanding neutrinos is one of the most pressing scientific issues in physics. She shares the latest neutrino discoveries that are exciting her and that could bring us new insights about the galactic centre

item.title: ScienceDaily: Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain
item.description: A surprising discovery suggests that some early signs of Alzheimer’s disease may begin outside the brain. Using miniature laboratory systems made from human cells, scientists found that genetic mutations associated with inherited Alzheimer’s can disrupt nerve-to-muscle connections without any involvement from the brain or spinal cord. This could help explain why some patients experience changes in balance, walking, and coordination long before memory problems develop.

item.title: ScienceDaily: After 40 years, CERN finds evidence of a one-in-10-billion particle decay
item.description: CERN scientists have finally found evidence of a particle decay so rare that it happens only once in roughly 10 billion decays, ending a search spanning more than 40 years. The breakthrough could help physicists uncover hidden particles and forces that lie beyond the reach of today's most powerful accelerators.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists finally discover why we learn to love bitter coffee
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a hidden gut-to-brain dopamine pathway that helps explain why bitter coffee and other initially unpleasant flavors can become favorites over time. The discovery reveals how the brain learns to crave certain foods and could eventually lead to new ways of reshaping eating habits and food preferences.

item.title: New Scientist: Global carbon emissions set to fall in 2026 due to Iran energy shock
item.description: Carbon dioxide emissions are projected to fall 0.4 per cent this year, driven in part by higher oil prices resulting from disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz

item.title: Nature: How to make failure your friend and teacher in science
item.description: Nature, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03654-3 Apprentices develop expertise after doing monotonous tasks repeatedly and learning from their mistakes. Scientists are no different, argues Ruth Morgan.

item.title: New Scientist: Cold therapy may be worse than doing nothing for post-exercise recovery
item.description: Many are convinced that ice baths or cold showers are an effective way to speed recovery after exercise, but a study finds that cold therapy may actually have the opposite effect

item.title: New Scientist: A true paleo diet would include a lot more insects
item.description: When we talk about prehistoric foods, we often focus on meat or perhaps cereal grains. But columnist Michael Marshall finds that ancient humans may have dined on more insects than we previously thought

item.title: Nature: He spent a year on ‘Mars’: NASA science officer emerges from mock mission
item.description: Nature, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03588-w Engineer Matthew Montgomery, who just finished a 378-day simulated Mars mission, talks about what it was like to be out of contact with the rest of humanity for a two-week blackout.

item.title: New Scientist: X chromosome gene may reduce autism rates in women and girls
item.description: A gene called ZFX exerts powerful effects on an entire network of genes linked to autism, which may help explain why the condition is less common in females

item.title: New Scientist: Is Schrödinger’s cat both dead and alive? No, it’s just haunted by its past
item.description: A radical new approach suggests some of quantum theory’s most bizarre and inexplicable effects might be down to physics failing to account properly for time

item.description: Nature, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02903-9 Looking for a postdoc while raising four children made one thing clear to Wenhuan Xu: many adverts describe the ideal applicant much more clearly than they describe the job itself.

item.title: New Scientist: Prehistoric Britons may have made giant stone axes to show off
item.description: Unusually large handaxes weighing up to 3 kilograms have puzzled archaeologists because they are so unwieldy, but their function may have been purely symbolic

item.title: Nature: How academic freedom is changing around the world — by the numbers
item.description: Nature, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02998-0 Nature reports on five countries where academic freedom either plummeted or soared in recent years.

item.title: Nature: Carlo Rovelli says fundamental physics is overrated
item.description: Nature, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03626-7 The theoretical physicist unpacks the need for more humility in science and whether artificial intelligence could ever become conscious.

item.title: New Scientist: Weird ‘ultraquantum’ turbulence seen for the first time
item.description: An experiment with ultracold potassium atoms has revealed details of a type of turbulence that only exists in the quantum realm and relies on odd tangles of stringy whirlpools

item.title: ScienceDaily: Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover
item.description: Scientists have discovered that pantethine, a readily available vitamin B5 derivative, can calm overactive immune cells and may help fight psoriasis. The supplement prevented psoriasis in mice and showed promising results in a small human trial, revealing an unexpected connection between cholesterol and autoimmune inflammation.

item.title: ScienceDaily: When your gut bacteria run out of fiber, they may start eating your gut lining
item.description: Scientists have discovered that gut bacteria can feed on the protective mucus lining your intestines, producing potentially harmful compounds, but fiber helps keep this activity in check. Overlooked proteins in plant foods also help shift gut bacteria toward producing beneficial substances, revealing a surprising new reason plant-based diets may be good for you.

item.title: ScienceDaily: A quantum breakthrough makes light behave like both a solid and a liquid
item.description: Scientists have observed a bizarre quantum state of matter that combines the structure of a crystal with the frictionless flow of a liquid, all at room temperature. The breakthrough overturns a major practical limitation of exotic quantum experiments and could help bring powerful new light-based computing and sensing technologies closer to reality.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists discover a surprising link between acorns and lyme disease
item.description: After more than 35 years of research, scientists have uncovered surprising clues about what really drives Lyme disease risk. Contrary to longstanding assumptions, deer populations appear less important than mice, which can fuel a 40% increase in tick numbers the following year. Even acorn production can predict tick population surges two years in advance, while extreme temperatures may be far less deadly to ticks than scientists once believed.

item.title: ScienceDaily: A simple supplement may help clear brain fog after cancer
item.description: A surprising new study from UCLA suggests that a naturally occurring molecule could help breast cancer survivors overcome the frustrating brain fog and exhaustion that can linger long after treatment ends. Researchers found that women taking an oxaloacetate supplement for eight weeks experienced substantial improvements in memory, concentration, mental clarity, and fatigue.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Caltech robot makes history by building a structure in space
item.description: For the first time, a robot has autonomously built part of a structure in space, demonstrating a breakthrough that could fundamentally change space exploration. The technology could one day allow scientists to construct enormous telescopes, communications antennas, and solar power stations in orbit, far beyond the size limits of today's rockets.

item.title: ScienceDaily: NASA reveals bold new plan to return astronauts to the Moon in 2028
item.description: NASA has revealed an accelerated plan to land astronauts on the Moon in 2028, with SpaceX and Blue Origin developing competing lunar landers and a crucial orbital test scheduled for 2027. Faster rocket preparations, new lightweight spacesuits, and redesigned missions could help pave the way for a permanent lunar presence and future human exploration of Mars.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Common osteoporosis drugs linked to 24% lower dementia risk in major study
item.description: A massive study of more than 120,000 older adults suggests that common osteoporosis drugs may reduce the risk of Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias by up to 24%. The surprising findings raise the possibility that medications already used to strengthen bones could also help protect the aging brain.

item.title: ScienceDaily: DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets
item.description: The Shroud of Turin, one of history's most mysterious religious artifacts, is yielding surprising new clues through DNA analysis. Scientists have uncovered a complex mixture of biological traces that may reveal more about the cloth's past and the environments it encountered. The findings offer a fresh scientific perspective on a centuries-old mystery that continues to spark fascination and debate.

item.title: Nature: The super El Niño is more than a climate shock – it’s a health one, too
item.description: Nature, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03628-5 Food shortages and disease outbreaks are to be expected and need to be addressed together.

item.title: Nature: Daily briefing: Ancient cave art found hiding in plain sight
item.description: Nature, Published online: 06 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03648-1 Rock-art in a Spanish cave dates back 26,000 years. Plus, flexible working policies can end up saddling academic mothers with more work and the origins of Celtic and Germanic languages.

item.title: Nature: AI has transformed maths — this is how we got here
item.description: Nature, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03627-6 The story of how maths came to run the world, and created the artificial-intelligence models that might surpass human mathematicians.

item.title: Nature: COP31 kicks off as planet faces imminent overshoot of 1.5°C climate target
item.description: Nature, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03631-w Scientists say governments must commit to carbon dioxide removal if world is to bring temperatures back down to safer limits.

item.title: ScienceDaily: A little-known protein could be a major culprit in type 2 diabetes
item.description: Scientists have discovered that a buildup of a protein called Miro1 may be a hidden driver of insulin resistance in Type 2 diabetes, with preclinical experiments showing that removing it restores the muscles’ response to insulin. Exercise was also found to lower Miro1 levels in people with diabetes, revealing a potential new pathway for treating the disease.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
item.description: Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of underwater “marine snow” plays a surprisingly important role in how much carbon reaches the deep ocean. Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists discover stunning new Amazon fish that may already be endangered
item.description: Researchers have discovered a stunning new species of tiny orange-patterned fish in the Brazilian Amazon, but its survival may already be at risk. Named Laimosemion laranja, the brilliantly colored killifish measures less than three centimeters long and was found in just three small forest pools. Its extremely limited habitat is threatened by mining, deforestation, pollution, and expanding development.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists wipe out deadly brain tumors in every mouse tested with new cancer therapy
item.description: Scientists at UC San Francisco have developed a powerful new cancer therapy that remains inactive until it reaches the brain, where it switches on to attack deadly tumors. The engineered immune cells, called B-SYNC CAR-T cells, completely eliminated diffuse midline glioma (DMG), an aggressive childhood brain cancer that is almost always fatal within a year, in two mouse models.

item.title: ScienceDaily: An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution
item.description: A remarkable fossil discovery in Colombia is challenging how scientists understand major evolutionary changes in Earth's history. Researchers uncovered an incredibly diverse ancient marine ecosystem where giant reptiles, sharks, and other creatures thrived as older evolutionary groups approached extinction and newer ones emerged. They call this previously unrecognized pattern a "Biotic Inflection," suggesting that major transformations in life can occur without mass extinctions.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Einstein's equations reveal how gravity could break, reconnect, and release energy
item.description: More than a century after Einstein revolutionized our understanding of gravity, scientists have uncovered a surprising new phenomenon hidden within his equations. Researchers at Columbia University and Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez have identified a theoretical process called "gravitational reconnection," in which structures within gravitational fields can break apart and reconnect, transferring energy into matter.

item.title: ScienceDaily: A 24-hour fast triggers a surprising repair response in the gut
item.description: Scientists have discovered that fasting for just 24 hours increases a beneficial gut bacterium that helps the intestines regenerate after radiation damage. The preclinical findings could pave the way for new treatments that protect healthy tissue during cancer therapy, potentially without requiring patients to fast.

item.title: ScienceDaily: MIT scientists turn immune cells into cancer killers inside the body
item.description: MIT scientists have developed nanoparticles that reprogram immune cells directly inside the body to attack cancer and harmful immune cells, eliminating tumors and reversing liver damage in mouse experiments. The breakthrough could make powerful immune therapies dramatically simpler and less expensive while opening new possibilities for treating cancer and autoimmune diseases.

item.title: ScienceDaily: A nuclear blast could save Earth from an asteroid, but there's a catch
item.description: A nuclear explosion might save Earth from a deadly asteroid, but new research suggests that hitting the wrong side could make the difference between success and disaster. Scientists found that an asteroid's irregular shape can dramatically affect how it responds to an X-ray blast, with deflection effectiveness varying nearly fivefold depending on the angle.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Low testosterone linked to 18% higher risk of dying from cancer
item.description: A major international study tracking more than 26,000 men found that very low testosterone levels were associated with an 18% higher risk of dying from cancer later in life. Surprisingly, testosterone itself showed no clear link to prostate cancer, although two other sex hormones did. Researchers believe low testosterone could be an important early warning sign of future health risks, particularly when levels fall below 8.6 nmol/L.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Ancient Siberian tomb reveals surprising secrets of cannabis use 2,800 years ago
item.description: Scientists investigating a 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb discovered roughly 1,000 cannabis seeds and chemical evidence suggesting ancient Scythians used the plant for its intoxicating effects. The remarkable find, surrounded by evidence of elaborate burial rituals and animal sacrifices, offers the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence of psychoactive cannabis use.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists discover hidden brain changes linked to common sleep disorders
item.description: Scientists have discovered that sleep disorders are associated with structural changes in brain regions that control attention, decision-making, and emotions, potentially explaining why disrupted sleep can affect everyday thinking and behavior. The findings, drawn from 57 brain imaging studies, reveal both shared and disorder-specific patterns that could lead to more targeted treatments.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists squeeze record-breaking X-ray power into an incredibly tiny spot
item.description: Scientists have created record-breaking X-ray flashes lasting just 300 attoseconds, concentrating enormous power into an incredibly tiny spot. The breakthrough could unlock a new way to observe electrons in action and potentially control the ultrafast processes that drive chemical reactions.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Stronger flu shot linked to nearly 55% lower Alzheimer's risk
item.description: A surprising new study suggests that a stronger flu shot could offer older adults significantly greater protection against Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at UTHealth Houston analyzed nearly 200,000 adults ages 65 and older and found that those who received a high-dose influenza vaccine had a nearly 55% lower risk of developing Alzheimer's, compared with a 40% reduction previously associated with the standard-dose vaccine.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists discover a hidden warning sign of cannabis addiction
item.description: A study of more than 17,700 US adults found that people who use cannabis in multiple forms have dramatically higher rates of daily consumption and addiction symptoms than those who stick primarily to one method. Nearly 67% of those who used almost every form met criteria for cannabis use disorder, compared with just 15% of people who mainly consumed edibles.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Mysterious gas leaks suggest Mars may still be volcanically alive
item.description: Mysterious gas emissions and fresh volcanic fissures suggest that Mars may not be geologically dead after all, with hot magma potentially still active deep underground. The discovery could point to hidden pockets of warmth and chemical energy capable of supporting microbial life beneath the Red Planet’s surface.

item.title: ScienceDaily: A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
item.description: Scientists have discovered a surprising quantum limit that prevents electrons from being tracked with unlimited precision in both space and time. The breakthrough could pave the way for manipulating chemical reactions and developing electronics hundreds of thousands of times faster than today's technology.

item.title: New Scientist: Antipersonnel mines have returned in Ukraine and now threaten the world
item.description: 3D printing, microcontrollers and drones have enabled the resurgence of antipersonnel mines in the Russia-Ukraine war, making mines deadlier and more accessible

item.title: ScienceDaily: Drinking 2–3 cups of coffee a day linked to dramatically lower dementia risk
item.description: Drinking two to three cups of caffeinated coffee daily was linked to a dramatically lower risk of dementia and better cognitive functioning in a study spanning up to 43 years. The benefits appeared regardless of genetic risk, but decaffeinated coffee did not show the same association.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Human bodies produce 2 billion metric tons of CO2 a year just by staying alive
item.description: Humans collectively produce more than 2 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide annually just by turning food into energy, a 74% increase over three decades largely driven by population growth. Unlike fossil fuel emissions, however, the CO2 we exhale is part of the natural carbon cycle, and scientists say measuring it more accurately could improve climate models.

item.title: New Scientist: COP climate summits might yet have a useful future – here’s how
item.description: No one is expecting COP31 to save the world from climate disaster, but it could provide a small taste of how international meetings can still deliver meaningful progress

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists discover Europe's ancient forests were nothing like we imagined
item.description: Scientists have uncovered evidence that Europe was dominated for more than 20 million years by open woodlands, colorful meadows, and large grazing animals, not the dense forests long considered its natural state. The surprising discovery challenges modern reforestation strategies, suggesting that planting thick forests could actually harm the biodiversity conservationists hope to protect.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Rubin Observatory discovers two hidden companions of the Milky Way. Hundreds more may be waiting
item.description: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory has already uncovered two previously unknown companions of the Milky Way using preliminary observations covering just 7% of the night sky. The discoveries include an extremely faint galaxy 355,000 light-years away and a star cluster hidden behind cosmic dust. Scientists suspect hundreds of additional satellite galaxies remain undiscovered, and Rubin's powerful telescope could finally bring them into view.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Magic mushrooms rewire the brain in a way scientists didn't expect
item.description: A surprising discovery reveals how psilocybin, the active compound in magic mushrooms, rapidly reshapes the brain by creating new neural connections and strengthening them. Researchers found that the drug behaves differently in healthy and chronically stressed mice, potentially helping repair brain circuits damaged by prolonged stress. Most intriguingly, they identified a way to trigger this brain rewiring without the behavioral response associated with psychedelic effects.

item.title: ScienceDaily: A compound hidden in broccoli could help fight a devastating genetic disease
item.description: A compound naturally found in broccoli could help fight Friedreich ataxia, a devastating genetic disease that progressively damages the nervous system, by boosting a vital protein and protecting nerve cells. Scientists hope the discovery could lead to an affordable treatment, although clinical trials are still needed to establish its effectiveness in patients.

item.title: ScienceDaily: A dead star's mysterious rings reveal what could happen when our Sun dies
item.description: Astronomers have discovered a strange double ring of planetary wreckage around a dead star, revealing a possible preview of our Solar System's distant future. The two rings are separated by a mysterious gap that researchers believe is maintained by surviving planetary bodies, including one potentially as large as Pluto or the Moon. Their different chemical compositions suggest they may contain the remains of separate destroyed planets.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists accidentally solve a chemistry mystery that lasted 60 years
item.description: After more than 60 years of unsuccessful attempts, scientists have finally isolated stable examples of elusive boron-oxygen molecules once considered too unstable to capture. The surprising breakthrough, achieved using relatively simple chemical reactions, could pave the way for an entirely new class of exotic compounds.

item.title: Nature: In Vivo CRISPR Base Editing of ANGPTL3 for Durable Lipid Lowering
item.description: Nature, Published online: 06 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11233-9 In Vivo CRISPR Base Editing of ANGPTL3 for Durable Lipid Lowering

item.title: New Scientist: Record-breaking, fast-spinning magnet could help uncover new physics
item.description: A magnet barely wider than a human hair is one of the fastest spinning objects ever and could be useful for both fundamental physics experiments and in quantum technology

item.title: New Scientist: An unexpected feedback loop may be driving mega heatwaves
item.description: Dry soil and high pressure can amplify extreme heat, helping to explain why regions like Europe are suffering record-shattering heatwaves much earlier than climate models predicted

item.title: Nature: These AI agents design your perfect robot-powered lab — and run it for you
item.description: Nature, Published online: 06 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03587-x A team of artificial-intelligence agents simulates a laboratory of robots and instruments to ensure that the physical workspace functions smoothly and then directs that workspace’s operations.

item.title: Nature: Briefing Chat: Meet the snakes that cartwheel away from trouble
item.description: Nature, Published online: 06 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03632-9 Nature staff discuss an acrobatic reptile defence strategy — plus, evidence of fossilized dinosaur blood cells.

item.title: New Scientist: Less than 4 minutes of vigorous exercise a day could halve your dementia risk
item.description: Bursts of vigorous physical activity, such as carrying heavy shopping or rushing for the bus, seem to have a significant effect on our brain health and dementia risk

item.title: New Scientist: Parkinson’s may be driven by ‘vicious cycle’ that disrupts brain waste drainage
item.description: Parkinson's disease is linked to toxic protein clumps and disrupted brain waste removal, which may feed off each other, causing the condition to progress

item.title: Nature: Cholera bacterium’s good deed: inspiring a glue with rare properties
item.description: Nature, Published online: 06 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03630-x An adhesive that binds strongly even under water was inspired by a protein made by a feared pathogen.

item.title: Nature: Medicinal plants, lessons from mushrooms and the power of smell: Books in brief
item.description: Nature, Published online: 06 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03595-x Andrew Robinson reviews five of the best science picks.

item.title: Nature: Preprint platform offers to pay researchers to review papers, but questions remain
item.description: Nature, Published online: 06 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03442-z A reviewer can earn US$200 through XSci’s scheme if they deliver their work within five days.

item.title: Nature: ‘Mathematics is more than a mechanical process’ — why I think the field will survive OpenAI’s disruption
item.description: Nature, Published online: 06 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03622-x Artificial intelligence could take the field into new territory, but researchers must create the rules and institutions that keep humans at its centre.

item.title: New Scientist: Hubble Space Telescope is falling to Earth – should NASA save it?
item.description: The Hubble Space Telescope faces a fiery and fatal re-entry to Earth's atmosphere sometime around 2032, but NASA is asking the private sector for ideas to keep it working

item.title: Nature: ESC (DC)2
item.description: Nature, Published online: 06 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03450-z Security issues.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
item.description: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Major trial challenges how doctors decide who really needs statins
item.description: A study of nearly 5,800 adults found that heart scans measuring calcium buildup in the arteries led to the same observed rate of major cardiovascular events as traditional risk assessments, despite recommending statins to far fewer patients. Surprisingly, patients advised to take statins based on their scans were nearly three times as likely to stick with their medication, raising intriguing questions about how doctors should identify and treat heart disease risk.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Five-inch-long beetle larvae are quietly destroying blueberry roots
item.description: Scientists have solved a mystery surrounding destructive beetles attacking blueberry bushes in North Carolina, identifying a species whose massive larvae can grow up to five inches long and destroy plant roots. Although farmers have reported damage for more than a decade, the insects responsible remained unidentified until researchers used DNA analysis to uncover the culprit.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Don't miss: Meteor showers, fireballs, and a supermoon light up November's night sky
item.description: November's night sky is packed with celestial wonders, from bright meteor fireballs and a close pairing of Mars and Jupiter to a spectacular supermoon. Meanwhile, NASA's Voyager 1 is making history by becoming the first spacecraft to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth.

item.title: ScienceDaily: NASA’s Swift telescope falls to Earth after nearly 22 years in space
item.description: After nearly 22 years of exploring the universe’s most violent explosions, NASA’s Swift Observatory has re-entered Earth’s atmosphere over Indonesia. Originally designed to last just two years, the pioneering space telescope transformed our understanding of black holes, exploding stars, and mysterious cosmic outbursts.

item.title: ScienceDaily: For decades, we were told to avoid full-fat dairy. New research says otherwise
item.description: Full-fat dairy may not be the health villain it has long been portrayed as, according to a new study finding that three daily servings did not worsen weight, cholesterol, or insulin resistance over 12 weeks. Researchers also observed improvements in blood pressure and nutrient intake, raising questions about longstanding recommendations to choose low-fat dairy.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Dead stars could break one of physics' most famous limits
item.description: A surprising new discovery suggests that some dead stars can grow far more massive than scientists once thought possible. Computer simulations show that powerful magnetic fields could allow white dwarfs to reach 2.4 times the mass of the Sun, dramatically exceeding a famous limit that has stood for decades. The findings could help explain unusually bright supernova explosions that have long puzzled astronomers.

item.title: ScienceDaily: An anti-aging drug may help protect the brain before Alzheimer's symptoms begin
item.description: A surprising new study suggests that an anti-aging drug could help protect people genetically predisposed to Alzheimer's disease. Researchers found that just four weeks of low-dose rapamycin improved brain blood flow in healthy middle-aged adults carrying the high-risk APOE4 gene variant, with women showing the strongest benefits. Because declining blood flow can occur years before Alzheimer's symptoms appear, the discovery raises hopes for preventing or delaying the disease before memory loss…

item.title: Nature: The palaeo cave art that hid in plain sight for 26,000 years
item.description: Nature, Published online: 06 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03585-z Hundreds of engravings were spotted in a widely visited cave — some include signs of animation.

item.title: Nature: Daily briefing: Toothbrush zaps bacteria to clear plaque
item.description: Nature, Published online: 05 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03596-w The manual toothbrush cleans by generating a bacteria-killing electrical charge. Plus, what ‘historic’ US mid-term results mean for science and a genetics lab run by AI-powered robots.

item.title: New Scientist: A robot called GIMLI will explore a lunar cave for a future moon base
item.description: The race to build a moon base is ramping up. Columnist Robin George Andrews explores how NASA is preparing by sending a cave-hunting robot ahead of humans

item.title: New Scientist: The economic benefits of the covid vaccines may be double what we thought
item.description: The global health and economic benefits of the covid-19 vaccines were thought to have reached up to $38 trillion in their first year, but a new analysis suggests $64.3 trillion is a more accurate figure

item.title: New Scientist: Tomb in Siberia reveals humans were using cannabis 2800 years ago
item.description: Psychoactive compounds have been found in a hair from a Scythian tomb in Siberia, providing the earliest direct evidence of cannabis being used as a drug

item.title: New Scientist: Google shouldn’t be pressuring schools to use its AI
item.description: Google has said schools can’t have access to its search engine without AI, even in schools where AI use is being banned. Columnist Jacob Aron says the tech giant shouldn’t be dictating education policy in this way
